pr_title: core: set fs.file-max sysctl to LONG_MAX rather than ULONG_MAX
pr_body:
Since kernel 5.2 the kernel thankfully returns proper errors when we
write a value out of range to the sysctl. Which however breaks writing
ULONG_MAX to request the maximum value. Hence let's write the new
maximum value instead, LONG_MAX.

/cc @brauner

Fixes: #12803
pr_comments:
@poettering  This affects also:
- [ linux 5.1](https://github.com/gregkh/linux/commit/33bc00a54dbcde976a9d927ddaac5a3266de317f)
- [linux 4.19](https://github.com/gregkh/linux/commit/91ae202e2c88a026eb2065fbee10b8e80591a27d)
- [linux 4.14](https://github.com/gregkh/linux/commit/869febe16b3e18bc908e66e8798185842f007f24)

so I think the comment should be adjusted and patch backported to systemd-stable.

We generally don't document who backported what where in our comments. That's just noise. It's interesting to know when things roughly changed, but beyond that we don't have to include a full version table really here, sorry.

If you thnk this should be backported to the systemd-stable tree, then please file a request there.

issue_context.title: "Failed to bump fs.file-max, ignoring: Invalid argument" after kernel upgraded from 5.1.9 to 5.1.10
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
> 242.29

<!-- **NOTE:** Do not submit bug reports about anything but the two most recently released systemd versions upstream! -->
<!-- For older version please use distribution trackers (see https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/master/docs/CONTRIBUTING.md#filing-issues). -->

**Used distribution**
 > Archlinux

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**
 > fs.file-max bumped.

**Unexpected behaviour you saw**
 > "Failed to bump fs.file-max, ignoring: Invalid argument" in dmesg

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
upgrade kernel from 5.1.9 to 5.1.10.

kernel config: [config.gz](https://github.com/systemd/systemd/files/3293778/config.gz)
comments:
5.1.10 contains this patch: sysctl: return -EINVAL if val violates minmax
https://lkml.org/lkml/2019/6/1/307

Seem related.
So, at least, this is not our bug, as we just write configured values. Can I close this?

review_comments: That comment is bit misleading. The maximum was always the same, it's just that before the error was squashed and now its reported. I think it'd be good to reword the comment. Also, typo: "thing were".

Na, the error wasn't just squashed. instead the kerne apparently parsed ULONG_MAX as LONG_MAX, either due to saturation, or due to some casting weirdness... I left this vague on purpose, since I didn't want to do code spelunking to figure out the details... but iirc the previous behaviour was that ULONG_MAX meant LONG_MAX, but ULONG_MAX+1 was not parsed at all... hence there's a differene between "maximum accepted" and "maximum configurable". it would accept something larger than was actually used.

`file-max` needs to be calculated via percpu counters. Those percpu counters are `long`s and not `unsigned long`s so it is not possible for `file-max` to ever go up to `unsigned long`. This restriction could technically be lifted but would require a new percpu api and then you also get trouble with how correct everything is going to be etc. pp. So `file-max` was always `long`. It really wasn't documented clearly anywhere though.

yes, internally in the kernel it was "signed long" all the time, just the kernel's sysctl parser perviously parsed values in the range LONG_MAX+1…ULONG_MAX as something weird, and now (correctly) doesn't anymore. Previously only ULONG_MAX+1…∞ where refused.
Yeah, just providing some more context. :)
OK. I admit I looked at the kernel patch briefly, but it's far from obvious.
